claim: 22 human subjects participated in Experiment 1 (Collins and Koechlin, 2012).
source: We modeled a specific human experiment for concurrent task-set monitoring, previously reported in Collins and Koechlin (2012); Donoso et al. (2014). The detail of the experimental procedures can be found in the original papers, here we provide only a summary. Data from Collins and Koechlin (2012) are called Experiment 1. Data from Donoso et al. (2014) are called Experiment 2. The experimental designs are identical. Experiment one is a behavioral experiment including 22 subjects.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of subjects in Experiment 1.

claim: 40 subjects participated in Experiment 2 (Donoso et al., 2014) with fMRI acquisition.
source: Experiment 2 involves 40 subjects, with fMRI acquisition.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of subjects and the use of fMRI in Experiment 2.

claim: Subjects had to learn associations between 3 digits and 4 letters by trial and error.
source: Subjects had to search for implicit associations between 3 digits and four letters by trial and error.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental task structure.

claim: Correct associations led to positive reward with 90% probability.
source: A correct association between the stimulus and the action led to positive reward with a probability 90%.
evidence: The manuscript specifies the reward probability for correct associations.

claim: Incorrect associations led to null reward with 90% probability.
source: An incorrect association between the stimulus and the action led to a null reward with a probability 90%.
evidence: The manuscript specifies the reward probability for incorrect associations.

claim: 10% of trials were misleading noisy trials.
source: 10% of (pseudo-randomized) trials were misleading noisy trials, yielding to a positive reward for an incorrect association, and vice-versa.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage of misleading trials.

claim: The correct set of responses remained unchanged over blocks of 36 to 54 trials (episodes).
source: The correct set of responses to stimuli remained unchanged over a block of 36 to 54 trials. Such a block is called an episode.
evidence: The manuscript describes the episode structure.

claim: Episode switches were not explicitly cued.
source: The transition from one episode to another is called an episode switch and was not explicitly cued.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design.

claim: Task-sets were always non-overlapping from one episode to another.
source: Task-sets were always non-overlapping from one episode to the other, that is each and every of the three stimulus-response associations differ after an episode switch.
evidence: The manuscript describes the task-set structure.

claim: An experimental session consisted of 25 episodes for Experiment 1.
source: An experimental session was a succession of 25 episodes for Experiment 1, and 24 episodes for Experiment 2.
evidence: The manuscript specifies the number of episodes per session.

claim: An experimental session consisted of 24 episodes for Experiment 2.
source: An experimental session was a succession of 25 episodes for Experiment 1, and 24 episodes for Experiment 2.
evidence: The manuscript specifies the number of episodes per session.

claim: In the open-ended session, task-sets were different in each episode.
source: In the open-ended session, task-sets were different in each episode, so there was no possibility for the subject to retrieve and reuse a formerly learned one.
evidence: The manuscript describes the open-ended session structure.

claim: In the recurrent session, only 3 task-sets reoccurred across episodes.
source: In the recurrent session, only 3 task-sets reoccurred across episodes (Figure 1a), and subjects could reuse previously learned task-sets.
evidence: The manuscript describes the recurrent session structure.

claim: Subjects were not informed about the distinction between the two sessions.
source: Subjects were not informed about the distinction between the two sessions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The proportion of correct responses to stimuli seen for the first time after the first correct response in an episode was significantly higher in the recurrent session compared to the open-ended session for the second stimulus (0.53 ± 0.05 vs 0.39 ± 0.04, t = 2.1, p=0.049).
source: The performance averaged over all subjects was significantly higher in the recurrent session compared to the open-ended session (T-test on related samples, second stimulus: 0.53 ± 0.05 vs 0.39 ± 0.04, t = 2.1, p=0.049; third stimulus: 0.65 ± 0.05 vs 0.46 ± 0.03, t = 3.1, p=0.0049), demonstrating that subjects exploited information from the correct response to a given stimulus to infer the correct response to other stimuli.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results comparing performance between sessions.

claim: The proportion of correct responses to stimuli seen for the first time after the first correct response in an episode was significantly higher in the recurrent session compared to the open-ended session for the third stimulus (0.65 ± 0.05 vs 0.46 ± 0.03, t = 3.1, p=0.0049).
source: The performance averaged over all subjects was significantly higher in the recurrent session compared to the open-ended session (T-test on related samples, second stimulus: 0.53 ± 0.05 vs 0.39 ± 0.04, t = 2.1, p=0.049; third stimulus: 0.65 ± 0.05 vs 0.46 ± 0.03, t = 3.1, p=0.0049), demonstrating that subjects exploited information from the correct response to a given stimulus to infer the correct response to other stimuli.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results comparing performance between sessions.

claim: Subjects do not modify their behavior following a misleading noisy feedback occurring late in an episode in the recurrent session (0.94 ± 0.01 before misleading feedback, 0.94 ± 0.01 after misleading feedback, t = 0.25, p=0.80).
source: An additional observation consistent with task-set learning was that subjects do not modify their behavior following a misleading noisy feedback occurring late in an episode (Figure 1c, recurrent session: 0.94 ± 0.01 before misleading feedback, 0.94 ± 0.01 after misleading feedback, t = 0.25, p=0.80 ; open-ended session 0.94 ± 0.01 before, 0.93 ± 0.01 after, t = 0.68, p=0.50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results for behavior following misleading feedback.

claim: Subjects do not modify their behavior following a misleading noisy feedback occurring late in an episode in the open-ended session (0.94 ± 0.01 before, 0.93 ± 0.01 after, t = 0.68, p=0.50).
source: An additional observation consistent with task-set learning was that subjects do not modify their behavior following a misleading noisy feedback occurring late in an episode (Figure 1c, recurrent session: 0.94 ± 0.01 before misleading feedback, 0.94 ± 0.01 after misleading feedback, t = 0.25, p=0.80 ; open-ended session 0.94 ± 0.01 before, 0.93 ± 0.01 after, t = 0.68, p=0.50).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results for behavior following misleading feedback.

claim: The network model consists of two subnetworks: the Associative Network (AN) and the Task-set Network (TN).
source: The model consisted of two subnetworks, which we refer to as the Associative Network (AN) and the Task-set Network (TN).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model architecture.

claim: The associative network consists of stimulus-selective populations and action-selective populations.
source: It consists of a set of stimulus-selective populations and a set of action-selective populations, the activity in each population being for simplicity binary (active or inactive).
evidence: The manuscript describes the associative network structure.

claim: Stimulus-action associations in the associative network are learned through reward-modulated plasticity.
source: The stimulus-action associations are learned through reward-modulated plasticity on the synapses between the two sets of populations (Fusi et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript describes the learning mechanism in the associative network, citing prior work.

claim: The task-set network consists of neural populations with mixed-selectivity to all conjunctions of stimuli and actions.
source: The task-set network consists of neural populations that display mixed-selectivity to all conjunctions of stimuli and actions (Rigotti et al., 2010b; Rigotti et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript describes the task-set network structure, citing prior work.

claim: Synapses between neural populations in the task-set network undergo temporal Hebbian learning.
source: Synapses between neural populations in the task-set network undergo temporal Hebbian learning, that is they are modified based on the successions of stimulus-response pairs produced by the associative network (Rigotti et al., 2010b; Ostojic and Fusi, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript describes the learning mechanism in the task-set network, citing prior work.

claim: Task-set learning can be achieved if the timescale of chunking is slower than the timescale of stimulus-response learning.
source: We first show that task-set learning can be achieved provided the timescale of chunking is slower than the timescale of stimulus-response learning.
evidence: The manuscript states a key finding from the model analysis.

claim: The presence of task-set inference improves network performance when the task-set network learning rate is slower than the associative network learning rate.
source: Our results show that the presence of task-set inference improves the network performance when the task-set network learning rate is slower than the associative network learning rate (red area in Figure 4a).
evidence: The manuscript reports model simulation results shown in Figure 4a.

claim: When learning in the task-set network is too fast, the network tracks noisy associations produced by the associative network.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3b,d,f,h, when learning in the task-set network is too fast, the network tracks noisy associations produced by the associative network, because of noise in the experimental feedback or because of errors made at the transition between episodes (blue area in Figure 4a).
evidence: The manuscript reports model simulation results shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In the open-ended session, the two models (with and without task-set inference) provided indistinguishable fits.
source: In the open-ended session, in which a given task-set never reoccurs between episodes, the two models provided indistinguishable fits.
evidence: The manuscript reports model fitting results.

claim: BOLD activity correlated positively with the inference signal strength in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, dorsal anterior cingulate cortex and anterior supplementary motor area in the recurrent session.
source: In the recurrent session (Figure 7—source data 1, bottom), BOLD activity correlated positively with the inference signal strength in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, dorsal anterior cingulate cortex and anterior supplementary motor area; and negatively in ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
evidence: The manuscript reports fMRI analysis results.

claim: BOLD activity correlated negatively with the inference signal strength in ventromedial prefrontal cortex in the recurrent session.
source: In the recurrent session (Figure 7—source data 1, bottom), BOLD activity correlated positively with the inference signal strength in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, dorsal anterior cingulate cortex and anterior supplementary motor area; and negatively in ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
evidence: The manuscript reports fMRI analysis results.

claim: In the open-ended session, no significant positive or negative effect in frontal lobes was found corresponding to the inference signal.
source: In contrast, in the open-ended session, we found no significant positive or negative effect in frontal lobes corresponding to this parametric modulator.
evidence: The manuscript reports fMRI analysis results.

claim: Task-set learning relies on unsupervised learning of temporal contiguity between events.
source: One hypothesis (Rigotti et al., 2010b) states that learning task-sets, and more generally rule-based behavior, relies on unsupervised learning of temporal contiguity between events.
evidence: The manuscript states a hypothesis from prior work.

claim: Events that occur repeatedly after each other are automatically associated as demonstrated in classical conditioning experiments.
source: Events that occur repeatedly after each other are automatically associated as demonstrated in classical conditioning experiments (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972; Hawkins et al., 1983; Rescorla, 1988; Sakai and Miyashita, 1991; Kahana, 1996; Yakovlev et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies demonstrating automatic association of temporally contiguous events.

claim: Hebbian synaptic plasticity can naturally lead to unsupervised learning of temporal contiguity between events.
source: Hebbian synaptic plasticity (Hebb, 1949) can naturally lead to such unsupervised learning of temporal contiguity between events (Földiák, 1991; Wallis et al., 1993; Griniasty et al., 1993; Fusi, 2002; Soltani and Wang, 2006; Blumenfeld et al., 2006; Fusi et al., 2007; Preminger et al., 2009; Li and DiCarlo, 2010; Ostojic and Fusi, 2013), and therefore provides a simple biological mechanism for learning task-sets (Rigotti et al., 2010b) and more generally model-based planning (Gershman et al., 2012; Russek et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting the role of Hebbian plasticity in temporal learning.

claim: Hebbian plasticity provides a simple biological mechanism for learning task-sets.
source: Hebbian synaptic plasticity (Hebb, 1949) can naturally lead to such unsupervised learning of temporal contiguity between events (Földiák, 1991; Wallis et al., 1993; Griniasty et al., 1993; Fusi, 2002; Soltani and Wang, 2006; Blumenfeld et al., 2006; Fusi et al., 2007; Preminger et al., 2009; Li and DiCarlo, 2010; Ostojic and Fusi, 2013), and therefore provides a simple biological mechanism for learning task-sets (Rigotti et al., 2010b) and more generally model-based planning (Gershman et al., 2012; Russek et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work proposing Hebbian plasticity as a mechanism for task-set learning.

claim: Fitting the two sessions together led to a small but significant degradation of fitting performance.
source: Fitting the two sessions together led to a small but significant degradation of fitting performance (Figure 5—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: The manuscript reports model fitting comparison results.

claim: Models fitted simultaneously on both sessions were not able to capture the sudden increase in performance revealing task-set retrieval after the first correct trial.
source: More importantly, the models fitted simultaneously on both sessions were not able to capture the sudden increase in performance revealing task-set retrieval after the first correct trial (Figure 5—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: The manuscript reports model fitting results.

claim: The model predicts that overlapping associations between task-sets induce a decrease in performance on the following trial.
source: In both cases, our model predicts that the overlapping association induces a decrease in performance on the following trial.
evidence: The manuscript describes model predictions for overlapping task-sets.

claim: Ventromedial prefrontal cortex and striatal activity correlate positively with prediction error in both recurrent and open-ended sessions.
source: As expected from previous studies (Tanaka et al., 2004; O'Doherty et al., 2004; Daw et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2006; Lebreton et al., 2009), we found ventromedial prefrontal cortex and striatal activity to correlate positively in the recurrent and in the open-ended session.
evidence: The manuscript reports fMRI analysis results consistent with prior literature.

claim: Positive correlations with synaptic strength of chosen association were found in striatum and ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
source: We found positive correlations in striatum and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and negative correlations in dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, anterior supplementary motor area and lateral prefrontal cortex, in both experimental sessions.
evidence: The manuscript reports fMRI analysis results.

claim: Negative correlations with synaptic strength of chosen association were found in dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, anterior supplementary motor area and lateral prefrontal cortex.
source: We found positive correlations in striatum and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and negative correlations in dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, anterior supplementary motor area and lateral prefrontal cortex, in both experimental sessions.
evidence: The manuscript reports fMRI analysis results.

claim: The dorsal system was engaged preferentially when the retrieval of a task-set was used to improve performance.
source: Comparing the model activity with BOLD signal allowed us to identify neural correlates of task-set retrieval in a functional network involving ventral and dorsal prefrontal cortex, with the dorsal system preferentially engaged when retrievals are used to improve performance.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes fMRI findings in the abstract.

claim: The model was not fitted on reaction times.
source: This provides a supplementary validation, as the model was not fitted on reaction times.
evidence: The manuscript describes the model fitting procedure.

claim: The model with inference predicted that the proportion of correct responses on chunked trials should be higher than on independent trials due to the inference signal implementing task-set retrieval.
source: The model with inference predicted that the proportion of correct responses on chunked trials should be higher than on independent trials due to the inference signal implementing task-set retrieval.
evidence: The manuscript describes a model prediction.

claim: In the model without inference, the performance on chunked and independent trials is indistinguishable.
source: In the model without inference where the associative network is independent of the task-set network, the performance on the two types of trials is instead indistinguishable.
evidence: The manuscript describes model behavior.

claim: The model predicted that incorrect task-set retrieval leads to a decrease of performance on the next trial after misleading feedback.
source: Our model predicted that in this case incorrect task-set retrieval leads to a decrease of the performance on the next trial.
evidence: The manuscript describes a model prediction.

claim: The two behaviors (retrieval of correct task-set and retrieval of incorrect task-set) cannot be predicted by the model without inference.
source: The two behaviors described above (retrieval of a correct task-set after the first correct response, and retrieval of an incorrect task-set after a misleading feedback) cannot be predicted by the model without inference: we thus assessed the generative performance of our chunking mechanism and falsified the model without inference (Palminteri et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes model comparison results.

claim: Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is specifically engaged for temporally integrating and organizing multimodal information.
source: Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is known to be specifically engaged for temporally integrating and organizing multimodal information (Miller, 2000; Duncan, 2001; Sakai, 2008; Kim et al., 2008; O'Reilly, 2010; Ma et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior literature on the role of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.

claim: Neurons in the anterior cingulate cortex monitor the allocation and intensity of control.
source: Previous work showed that neurons in the anterior cingulate cortex monitor the allocation and the intensity of control (Dosenbach et al., 2006; Behrens et al., 2007; Rushworth et al., 2007; Shenhav et al., 2013; Khamassi et al., 2013; Enel et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior literature on the role of anterior cingulate cortex.

claim: The dorsal anterior cingulate cortex was shown to be specifically selective to switch-in events in this experiment.
source: In this specific experiment, using a Bayesian framework, the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex was shown to be specifically selective to switch-in events (Donoso et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior analysis of the same experimental data.

claim: Mixed-selectivity response can be implemented through random projections from the associative network to the task-set network.
source: Such mixed-selectivity response can be implemented through random projections from the associative network to the task-set network (Rigotti et al., 2010a; Lindsay et al., 2017), which for simplicity we don't explicitly include in the model.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on implementing mixed-selectivity and describes model simplification.

claim: The equilibrium synaptic weights in the task-set network directly reflect the temporal contiguity between stimulus-response pairs.
source: The equilibrium synaptic weights in the task-set network therefore directly reflect the temporal contiguity between stimulus-response pairs (Ostojic and Fusi, 2013) and thus encode the task-sets.
evidence: The manuscript describes model properties, citing prior work.

claim: The equilibrium value of synaptic weights is an increasing function of the probability that two stimulus-response pairs follow each other and of the potentiation rate in the task-set network.
source: This equilibrium value is an increasing function of the probability that two stimulus-response pairs follow each other, and of the potentiation rate in the task-set network (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript describes model properties.

claim: The model is based on biologically constrained models but highly abstracted to allow for direct comparison with human behavioral data.
source: Here we adopted an approach that interpolates between these two extremes, and used an intermediate-level model, which was based on biologically constrained models, but highly abstracted to allow for direct comparison with human behavioral data.
evidence: The manuscript describes the modeling approach.

claim: The reward-dependent Hebbian learning and winner-take-all mechanisms in the associative network were based on previous studies in conditional associative learning.
source: The reward-dependent Hebbian learning and winner-take-all mechanisms in the associative network were based on previous studies in the field of conditional associative learning (Williams, 1992; Wang, 2002; Wong and Wang, 2006; Fusi et al., 2007; Soltani and Wang, 2010; Soltani et al., 2017; Hertz, 2018; Sutton and Barto, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work as the basis for model components.

claim: The temporal chunking mechanism in the task-set network was based on Hebbian plasticity at behavioral timescales.
source: The temporal chunking mechanism in the task-set network was based on Hebbian plasticity at behavioral timescales, and can be generated for instance through sustained neural activity and extended STDP (van Rossum et al., 2000; Compte et al., 2000; Miller and Cohen, 2001; Rougier et al., 2005; Drew and Abbott, 2006; Curtis and Lee, 2010; Murray et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work as the basis for model components.

claim: Mixed-selectivity has been widely observed in the prefrontal cortex.
source: The required mixed-selectivity can be obtained from randomly connected neurons receiving feed-forward inputs coming from sensory and motor areas and has been widely observed in the prefrontal cortex (Asaad et al., 1998; Wallis et al., 2001; Genovesio et al., 2005; Rigotti et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior empirical work demonstrating mixed-selectivity in prefrontal cortex.

claim: A biologically plausible instantiation of the gating mechanism remains an open question.
source: Ultimately, a biologically plausible instantiation of this gating remains an open question, as the currently available physiological data does not provide sufficient constraints.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation of current knowledge.

claim: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex correlated negatively with the inference signal, that is positively with the compatibility between encoding in the two subnetworks when a reward was received.
source: In particular, the ventromedial prefrontal cortex correlated negatively with the inference signal, that is positively with the compatibility between encoding in the two subnetworks when a reward was received (as a prediction error-like signal).
evidence: The manuscript interprets fMRI results.

claim: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex plays a role in monitoring the Bayesian actor reliability in this experiment.
source: This is potentially in accordance with the role of ventromedial prefrontal cortex in monitoring the Bayesian actor reliability in this experiment (Donoso et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior interpretation of the same experimental data.

claim: Temporal Hebbian learning on a hierarchy of different timescales may create chunks combining states, action, rewards, or more abstract 'task-sets' to create hierarchically more complex representations.
source: Temporal Hebbian learning on a hierarchy of different timescales may create chunks combining states, action, rewards, or more abstract 'task-sets' to create hierarchically more complex representations.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a theoretical extension of the model.

claim: This type of plasticity provides a potential mechanism for learning transition probabilities on complex state-space and suggests a candidate implementation of the successor representation.
source: Moreover, this type of plasticity provides a potential mechanism for learning transition probabilities on this complex state-space, and therefore suggests a candidate implementation the successor representation (with the augmentation of eligibility traces, [Gershman and Niv, 2012; Russek et al., 2017]) and multi-step transitions maps (Kahana, 1996).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a theoretical connection to other frameworks, citing prior work.

claim: Generalization could be produced by augmenting the network with a layer composed of neurons selective to combinations of three stimuli and three actions.
source: Augmenting our network with a generalization layer composed of neurons selective to the combination of three stimuli and three actions could produce faster learning of a new task-set by biasing lower cortical structures.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a theoretical extension of the model.

claim: Caching multi-steps transitions in a single value (model-free) or not (model-based) would be equivalent to learning at slower timescales in an increasingly complex hierarchy of cortex layers.
source: Caching multi-steps transitions in a single value (model-free) or not (model-based) would then be equivalent to learning at slower timescales in an increasingly complex hierarchy of cortex layers (Murray et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a theoretical interpretation, citing prior work.

claim: The brain relies on estimates of uncertainty within and between task-sets.
source: The brain relies on estimates of uncertainty within and between task-sets (Yu and Dayan, 2005; Courville et al., 2006; Collins and Koechlin, 2012; Rushworth and Behrens, 2008; Gershman et al., 2012; Kepecs and Mainen, 2012; Donoso et al., 2014; Soltani and Izquierdo, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior literature on uncertainty estimation in the brain.

claim: Collins and Koechlin (2012) showed that the Bayesian likelihood ('reliability') of each task-set in memory is evaluated.
source: More specifically, Collins and Koechlin (2012) have shown that the Bayesian likelihood ('reliability') of each task-set in memory is evaluated.
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific finding from prior work.

claim: Inferences on the current and alternative task-sets have been found to occur in medial and lateral prefrontal cortices respectively.
source: Inferences on the current and alternative task-sets have been found to occur in medial and lateral prefrontal cortices respectively Donoso et al. (2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific finding from prior work.

claim: The model was developed to test the specific hypothesis that task-set learning relies on Hebbian chunking of individual stimulus-response associations.
source: This model was moreover developed to test a specific hypothesis, namely that task-set learning relies on Hebbian chunking of individual stimulus-response associations.
evidence: The manuscript states the purpose of the model.

claim: The model included some basic biological constraints but was purposefully simplified to allow for straightforward fitting to human behavioral data.
source: While the model included some basic biological constraints, it was purposefully simplified to allow for straightforward fitting to human behavioral data on a subject-by-subject basis.
evidence: The manuscript describes the modeling approach.

claim: Both models were fitted to behavioral data using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE).
source: Both models were fitted to behavioral data using the standard maximum likelihood estimation (MLE).
evidence: The manuscript describes the fitting procedure.

claim: Parameters were estimated subject by subject.
source: Parameters were estimated subject by subject.
evidence: The manuscript describes the fitting procedure.

claim: The Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) was computed as the opposite of equation (4.139) of Bishop (2007).
source: Following Figure 2 of Collins and Koechlin (2012), the BIC was computed as the opposite of equation (4.139) of Bishop (2007).
evidence: The manuscript describes the method for computing BIC, citing a reference.

claim: A larger log-likelihood and lower BIC and AIC correspond to better model fits.
source: A larger log-likelihood and lower BIC and AIC correspond to best model fits.
evidence: The manuscript describes the interpretation of model comparison metrics.

claim: The AIC (Akaike information criterion) was also compared for both models and reached identical conclusions to BIC.
source: We also compared the AIC (Akaike information criterion) for both models and reached identical conclusions (see Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports additional model comparison results.

claim: Model simulations reproduced model fits and data, ensuring that the model is not overfitting subjects' data.
source: Model simulation reproduced model fits and data, which ensured that we are not overfitting subjects' data.
evidence: The manuscript describes model validation procedure.

claim: All parametric modulators were z-scored to ensure between regressor and between subjects commensurability.
source: All parametric modulators were z-scored to ensure between regressor and between subjects commensurability (Lebreton et al., 2019; see also Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes fMRI analysis preprocessing, citing a reference.

claim: Ventromedial prefrontal cortex and striatal activity correlate positively with prediction error, as expected from previous studies.
source: As expected from previous studies (Tanaka et al., 2004; O'Doherty et al., 2004; Daw et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2006; Lebreton et al., 2009), we found ventromedial prefrontal cortex and striatal activity to correlate positively in the recurrent and in the open-ended session.
evidence: The manuscript reports fMRI results consistent with prior literature.

claim: Positive correlations with synaptic strength of chosen association are consistent with previous findings in value-based decision making.
source: These results are consistent with previous findings in the field of value-based decision making (Tanaka et al., 2004; Daw et al., 2006; Lebreton et al., 2009; Chib et al., 2009; Alexander and Brown, 2011; Donoso et al., 2014; Neubert et al., 2015; Palminteri et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior literature consistent with the findings.

claim: ROIs were selected independently from the statistical maps of betas to ensure valid comparison.
source: This comparison was valid as soon as the region of interest is selected independently from the statistical maps of betas (Poldrack, 2007), that is the selected ROI need to be based on a different contrast than the one currently studied.
evidence: The manuscript describes the ROI selection procedure, citing a methodological reference.

claim: The functional network was defined by co-activations in both sessions for the trial-by-trial task-set network inference signal.
source: We defined a functional network by the co-activations in both sessions, for the trial-by-trial task-set network inference signal to the associative network (ANOVA REC+OE for dorsomedial and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, ANOVA -REC-OE for ventromedial prefrontal cortex, FWE 0.05, Table 1), which thus did not promote differences.
evidence: The manuscript describes the ROI definition procedure.

claim: Only regressors of synaptic strength at decision onset and positive rewards at feedback onset showed positive correlations in hippocampus in both sessions.
source: Only regressors of the synaptic strength of the chosen association at the onset decision, and of positive rewards at the onset feedback, showed positive correlations in both sessions, but the difference between sessions was not significant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports fMRI analysis results for hippocampus.

claim: The difference in hippocampal activation between sessions was not significant.
source: Only regressors of the synaptic strength of the chosen association at the onset decision, and of positive rewards at the onset feedback, showed positive correlations in both sessions, but the difference between sessions was not significant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports fMRI analysis results for hippocampus.

claim: Hippocampal activation is consistent with the general role of hippocampus in associative binding.
source: This is consistent with the general role of the hippocampus in associative binding (Davachi and DuBrow, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript interprets hippocampal results in light of prior literature.

claim: There was no significant activation of hippocampus corresponding to the task-set network inference signal in either session.
source: In contrast, there was no significant activation of hippocampus corresponding to the task-set network inference to the associative network, neither in the recurrent nor in the open-ended session.
evidence: The manuscript reports fMRI analysis results for hippocampus.

claim: The analysis regresses the value of the inference strength from the task-set network biasing the decision network while learning occurs, as a cognitive control signal.
source: Note that we are regressing the value of the inference strength from the task-set network biasing the decision network while learning occurs, as a cognitive control signal would do.
evidence: The manuscript clarifies the interpretation of the fMRI analysis.

claim: The analysis provides an indirect measure of memory encoding in the task-set network, instead of the actual value of synaptic weights.
source: It's an indirect measure of memory encoding in the task-set network, instead of the actual value of synaptic weights.
evidence: The manuscript clarifies the interpretation of the fMRI analysis.

claim: Code is available at https://github.com/florapython/TemporalChunkingTaskSets.
source: Code is available at https://github.com/florapython/TemporalChunkingTaskSets (Bouchacourt, 2020; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/TemporalChunkingTaskSets).
evidence: The manuscript provides code availability information.
